blocks.text: Hangar , together with the Fondation A Stichting , is one of the most important centres for photography in Brussels – so it goes without saying that they are a must-see at Paris Photo and during Luxembourg Art Week .

In Paris, Hangar is marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography: they are showcasing four artists who, through their own artistic practice, emphasise the vitality of the medium from creative exploration of processes to an innovative perspective on the vibrant reality

Later this month, as part of Luxembourg Art Week 2026, Hangar will showcase six artists who highlight the power of the medium of photography through stunning works centred on the themes of ‘landscape’ and ‘the transience of time’

Sylvie Bonnot (FR – 1982) continues to explore her distinctive practice of ‘moulting’ and demonstrates that, despite two centuries of research, it is still possible to develop a new silver-based photographic technique. She highlights the parallels between the exhaustion of the raw materials needed for photography and the depletion of water reserves. In her series ‘Prisme Liquide’, her ‘moultings’ either ripple gently or burst across the paper like a torrential downpour, occasionally leaving nothing but a few droplets of the image.

Antoine De Winter (BE – 1985) revives ancient and sometimes forgotten techniques from the early days of photography: cyanotype, anthracotype, and salt print. By incorporating rock or salt from the landscapes as pigments and adorning them with gold leaf, his works on glass become precious fragments of a place’s memory, the subject of his ongoing series All the places and the places between .

Véronique Ellena (FR – 1966), with her series Clairs Obscurs , praises the analogue negative, enlarged and presented as it is: light becomes shadow and shadow becomes light. The colours are not of this world but the reflection of a poetic inner world, a bridge between past and present, between painting and photography.

Alice Pallot (FR – 1995) presents a preview of her new series Birdwatchers (initiated as part of a commission from Louis Vuitton for its City Book New York 2027, in collaboration with Tendance Floue). Through her encounters with various birdwatching communities in New York, she explores birdwatching as a practice of mindfulness: a way of connecting with living things through patience, distance and contemplation, where the simple act of observing becomes a means of building a community and experiencing the city in a different way.

Lior Gal (FR/IL – 1977) works with silver gelatin prints depicting fragments of landscapes he encounters during long walks. Back in his studio, he wraps them with threads of various origins; the repetitive act of weaving evokes time and silence, conducive to meditation. Gradually, the threads obscure the image, introducing a visual disruption that contrasts with the immediacy of the photographic shot.

Kíra Krász (HU – 1995) continues her series From marble to stone . She revisits an abandoned Hungarian sculpture park, once a symbol of rebellion, and reflects on the life cycle of art and territories by creating silver gelatin prints on stone, or by ‘tending’ to the buildings depicted in her prints with medical gauze.

Matthieu Litt (BE – 1983) joined a scientific expedition navigating through the Arctic pole, once a Terra Nullius where explorators could claim virgin frozen lands, and which is now facing the fastest warming of temperatures around the globe. His medium format analogue multi-exposures blend accident and poetry, creating serene yet uncanny visions of a lost paradise.

Luc Praet (BE – 1966) has been developing is series ALTERED for the last ten years. He visits major museums all around the world to capture fragments of masterpieces with his camera. He then meticulously alters his prints to evoke the passing of time and the memory process while celebrating the legacy the great masters have left us.
Paris Photo from 12 to 15 November , in the Main Sector (booth A47), featuring the artists Sylvie Bonnot, Antoine De Winter, Véronique Ellena and Alice Pallot .
